chief_complaint: bright blood-red patch on white eye after coughing fit
hpi_details: A 56-year-old woman notices a sharply demarcated bright-red patch on the white of one eye immediately after a coughing fit. It is painless and her vision is unchanged; she has no trauma, photophobia, discharge, or contact-lens-related symptoms.
ideas: She thinks that coughing so violently popped a blood vessel on the surface of her eye.
concerns: She is worried that the sudden pool of blood means her blood pressure spiked dangerously high and she is about to have a stroke.
expectations: She hopes to have her eye pressure measured and be reassured that her vision is completely safe.

core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Subconjunctival hemorrhage is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Standard management emphasizes Plan for Subconjunctival Hemorrhage: Reassurance, resolves spontaneously in 2 weeks, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: bright blood-red patch on white eye after coughing fit

Key HPI features: A 56-year-old female presents to the clinic with bright blood-red patch on white eye after coughing fit. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
Objective/Exam findings: Document the affected eye, visual acuity, pupils, ocular motility, blood pressure, and extent of hemorrhage; look for trauma or a foreign body.
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Subconjunctival hemorrhage.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Conjunctivitis without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Missing ocular trauma, pain, photophobia, reduced vision, proptosis, abnormal pupil or motility, or a 360-degree hemorrhage, which require urgent ophthalmic assessment.
management_principles: For an uncomplicated spontaneous hemorrhage with normal vision, provide reassurance; it usually clears over 1 to 2 weeks and artificial tears may help irritation.
Check blood pressure and review trauma, recurrence, easy bruising, and antiplatelet or anticoagulant use; investigate recurrent or unexplained episodes as clinically indicated.
Arrange urgent same-day eye assessment for pain, photophobia, reduced vision, significant trauma, proptosis, limited eye movement, abnormal pupil, or circumferential hemorrhage.
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: Patient presenting with chief complaint of bright blood-red patch on white eye after coughing fit. HPI: subconjunctival hemorrhage.
reference_soap.objective: Record affected eye, visual acuity, pupils, ocular motility, blood pressure, and hemorrhage extent; assess for trauma or foreign body.
reference_soap.assessment: Condition highly suspicious for Subconjunctival Hemorrhage.
reference_soap.plan: If painless with normal vision and no trauma, reassure that it usually resolves in 1 to 2 weeks; artificial tears are optional. Check blood pressure and review bleeding risk. Urgently refer same day for pain, photophobia, reduced vision, trauma, proptosis, limited motility, abnormal pupil, or circumferential hemorrhage.

learning_objectives: Recognize clinical presentation and diagnostic markers of Subconjunctival Hemorrhage
Select appropriate diagnostic workup for Subconjunctival Hemorrhage
Implement evidence-based management plan: Reassurance, resolves spontaneously in 2 weeks

teaching.one_liner: Patient with a bright blood-red patch on the white of the eye after a coughing fit.
red_flags: Pain, photophobia, reduced vision, trauma, proptosis, limited eye movement, abnormal pupil, or hemorrhage around the entire cornea requires urgent same-day eye assessment
Recurrent or unexplained episodes warrant blood-pressure and bleeding-risk evaluation

must_ask.say: Is there any pain or just the redness?

must_ask.objective: Establish laterality and exclude vision-threatening symptoms
must_ask.say: Which eye is affected, and have you had any change in vision, light sensitivity, or eye pain?
Did this appear right after coughing?
Do you take any blood-thinning medications?

must_ask.objective: Exclude injury and assess bleeding risk
must_ask.say: Did anything hit or get into the eye, and have you noticed easy bruising or bleeding elsewhere?
Has this happened to you before?
This will resolve on its own over about two weeks without treatment.

No, it doesn't hurt at all, and there is no scratchiness or feeling like something is in my eye.

exam.finding: Alert, comfortable woman in no acute distress, with visible focal redness over the right sclera.
Blood pressure is 124/78 mmHg, heart rate 72 beats per minute, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, body temperature 36.6 °C, and oxygen saturation 99% on room air.
Sharply demarcated, bright red patch of blood on the temporal bulbar conjunctiva of the right eye with clear surrounding sclera and no discharge; left conjunctiva and sclera are normal.

Visual acuity is 20/20 in both eyes, pupils are equal, round, and briskly reactive to light without afferent defect, extraocular movements are full without pain, and the corneas are clear without abrasions or foreign bodies.
No preauricular, submandibular, or anterior cervical lymphadenopathy.
Clear breath sounds bilaterally on auscultation without wheezing, crackles, or rhonchi.
No rash, vesicles on the forehead or nose, petechiae, or purpuric lesions on the skin.
